note: A closed list. A model may select from it and may not extend it: an unmatched claim is recorded as unclassified, never as a new tag. Sector and industry are deterministic issuer attributes on the issuer entity, not tags here; the sector_context axis holds forces a manager argues about, which is a different thing. Every tag carries a negative example because the way a taxonomy rots is by a tag quietly widening until it means nothing.

tags.label: Acquisition programme
tags.definition: A repeatable acquisition strategy.
tags.positiveExample: They buy six distributors a year at 6x.

tags.label: Buyback
tags.definition: A stated repurchase programme.
tags.positiveExample: They are retiring 8% of shares a year.

tags.label: Deleveraging
tags.definition: A stated path to lower debt.
tags.positiveExample: Net debt falls from 3.1x to 1.5x by 2028.

tags.label: Divestiture
tags.definition: A stated intention to sell a business.
tags.positiveExample: The chemicals division is being marketed.

tags.label: Dividend policy
tags.definition: A stated dividend commitment or change.
tags.positiveExample: The dividend was raised 15% and covered twice.

tags.label: Asset value discount
tags.definition: The market price sits below a defensible appraisal of the assets.
tags.positiveExample: The property portfolio alone exceeds the market capitalisation.
tags.negativeExample: Earnings will grow faster than expected.

tags.label: Cyclical recovery
tags.definition: The thesis rests on a cycle turning, not on a structural change in the business.
tags.positiveExample: Orders have troughed and the next upcycle is not in the price.
tags.negativeExample: Demand is structurally higher for ever.

tags.label: Mispriced optionality
tags.definition: Value sits in an outcome the market assigns roughly zero probability.
tags.positiveExample: The market ascribes nothing to the second pipeline asset.

tags.label: Quality compounder
tags.definition: The manager owns it for durable high returns on capital reinvested over years, not for a re-rating.
tags.positiveExample: We expect this business to reinvest at 20% returns for a decade.
tags.negativeExample: The stock is cheap on next year's earnings.

tags.label: Special situation
tags.definition: The return depends on a discrete corporate event rather than operations.
tags.positiveExample: The spread to the agreed offer price is 8% over four months.
tags.negativeExample: Margins will expand over three years.

tags.label: Turnaround
tags.definition: A troubled business where the thesis is repair, under new management or a new plan.
tags.positiveExample: The new chief executive has closed the loss-making division.
tags.negativeExample: The business has compounded for twenty years.

tags.label: Contract award
tags.definition: A specific contract or award decision.
tags.positiveExample: The defence contract is decided in the fourth quarter.
tags.negativeExample: They have a strong order book.

tags.label: Corporate action
tags.definition: A spin-off, sale, merger or similar.
tags.positiveExample: The board has agreed to spin off the industrial unit.

tags.label: Earnings event
tags.definition: A scheduled results date expected to reveal the thesis.
tags.positiveExample: Q2 results in August should show the margin turn.

tags.label: Index or listing event
tags.definition: Inclusion, uplisting or a new venue.
tags.positiveExample: Index inclusion follows the June review.

tags.label: Product launch
tags.definition: A dated launch or approval.
tags.positiveExample: The new platform ships in March 2027.
tags.negativeExample: They have a strong product pipeline.

tags.label: Regulatory decision
tags.definition: A decision by a regulator on a known date or window.
tags.positiveExample: The regulator decides by 14 May 2027.

tags.label: Input cost cycle
tags.definition: Input prices moving the economics of the industry.
tags.positiveExample: Ethane at these levels adds four points to margin.

tags.label: Regulatory regime change
tags.definition: A change in the rules governing the industry.
tags.positiveExample: The new framework allows direct-to-consumer sales.

tags.label: Secular demand shift
tags.definition: A durable change in end demand, independent of the cycle.
tags.positiveExample: Data centre power demand is on a different trajectory.
tags.negativeExample: Demand is recovering from the trough.

tags.label: Capacity addition
tags.definition: New capacity that changes the earnings base.
tags.positiveExample: The third fab doubles wafer starts in 2027.
tags.negativeExample: They will invest in the business.

tags.label: Cost programme
tags.definition: A named, quantified cost reduction.
tags.positiveExample: They have committed to $400m of annualised savings by 2027.
tags.negativeExample: They intend to be more efficient.

tags.label: Margin inflection
tags.definition: Margins are expected to turn, and that turn carries the thesis.
tags.positiveExample: Gross margin should move from 31% to 38% as the new line fills.
tags.negativeExample: Margins have been stable for five years.

tags.label: Market share gain
tags.definition: Taking share from identified competitors.
tags.positiveExample: They have taken six points of share from the incumbent.

tags.label: Mix shift
tags.definition: A shift toward higher-value products or customers.
tags.positiveExample: Software is moving from 20% to 40% of revenue.
tags.negativeExample: All segments grow at the same rate.

tags.label: Volume growth
tags.definition: Units, not price, drive the case.
tags.positiveExample: Shipments should grow 18% as capacity comes on.

tags.label: Activist engagement
tags.definition: A public campaign or engagement by the manager.
tags.positiveExample: We have nominated three directors.

tags.label: Board change
tags.definition: Directors added, removed or sought.
tags.positiveExample: Two nominees joined the board in May.

tags.label: Control structure
tags.definition: Dual-class shares or a controlling holder.
tags.positiveExample: The founder holds 61% of the votes on 9% of the economics.

tags.label: Insider alignment
tags.definition: Insider ownership or purchases aligning incentives.
tags.positiveExample: The founder owns 22% and bought more in March.

tags.label: Management change
tags.definition: A named change in senior management.
tags.positiveExample: The new chief executive started in January.

tags.label: One to three years
tags.positiveExample: Over the next two to three years.

tags.label: Over five years
tags.positiveExample: We expect to own this for a decade.
tags.negativeExample: We expect a re-rating this year.

tags.label: Three to five years
tags.positiveExample: By the end of the decade.

tags.label: Under one year
tags.definition: The thesis resolves within twelve months.
tags.positiveExample: We expect this to play out by next summer.

tags.label: Commoditised
tags.definition: The product competes primarily on price.
tags.positiveExample: Pricing is set by the spot market.

tags.label: Durable moat
tags.definition: A structural barrier the manager expects to persist.
tags.positiveExample: Regulatory approval takes a competitor six years to obtain.
tags.negativeExample: The company is currently the largest player.

tags.label: Pricing power
tags.definition: The ability to raise price without losing volume.
tags.positiveExample: They raised price 9% and volume was flat.

tags.label: Scale advantage
tags.definition: Unit economics improve with size in a way rivals cannot match.
tags.positiveExample: Their cost per delivery falls as density rises.

tags.label: Switching costs
tags.definition: Customers face real cost or risk in leaving.
tags.positiveExample: Migrating the ledger would take a bank eighteen months.
tags.negativeExample: Customers are satisfied with the product.

tags.label: Competitive erosion
tags.definition: A named competitor threatens the economics.
tags.positiveExample: A new entrant is pricing 30% below.

tags.label: Customer concentration
tags.definition: A small number of customers carry the revenue.
tags.positiveExample: Two customers are 58% of revenue.

tags.label: Cyclical downturn
tags.definition: The cycle turning against the position.
tags.positiveExample: A housing slowdown would halve volumes.

tags.label: Execution risk
tags.definition: The plan may not be delivered.
tags.positiveExample: The integration has slipped twice already.

tags.label: Leverage risk
tags.definition: The balance sheet limits the manager's tolerance.
tags.positiveExample: Net debt is 4.6x EBITDA with a 2027 maturity.

tags.label: Litigation risk
tags.definition: Pending litigation with a material outcome.
tags.positiveExample: The patent suit could remove the lead product.

tags.label: Regulatory risk
tags.definition: A rule or ruling could impair the thesis.
tags.positiveExample: A price cap would remove a third of profit.

tags.label: Free cash flow yield support
tags.definition: A free cash flow yield the manager treats as a floor.
tags.positiveExample: A 9% free cash flow yield limits the downside.
tags.negativeExample: The company will be profitable next year.

tags.label: Growth at a reasonable price
tags.definition: Growth bought at a multiple the manager considers undemanding.
tags.positiveExample: 20% growth at 15x forward earnings.
tags.negativeExample: We paid up for the best business in the sector.

tags.label: Multiple re-rating
tags.definition: The thesis requires the multiple to rise, not just earnings.
tags.positiveExample: At 11x it should trade closer to the peer group's 17x.
tags.negativeExample: Earnings will double and the multiple will stay flat.

tags.label: Replacement value
tags.definition: Value anchored to what rebuilding the asset base would cost.
tags.positiveExample: A new plant would cost twice the enterprise value.
tags.negativeExample: The shares are cheap versus peers.

tags.label: Sum of the parts
tags.definition: Value is argued segment by segment.
tags.positiveExample: The services arm alone is worth the whole market capitalisation.
tags.negativeExample: The company trades below its historical average multiple.
